meta.description: Build and benchmark shared memory index

user.t:
You are the SHARED-MEMORY engineer for the Rust crate at C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh (read DESIGN.md). Goal: a fast shared vector memory that all agents in the mesh query, measured on lookup latency, recall and memory use — only claim improvement with numbers.

Toolchain: in every Bash call first run:
export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:/c/Users/mariu/AppData/Local/Microsoft/WinGet/Packages/BrechtSanders.WinLibs.POSIX.UCRT_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe/mingw64/bin:$PATH"

Other agents concurrently own src/hebbian.rs, baselines.rs, mesh.rs, main.rs, sim.rs, stats.rs, variants.rs, src/bin/experiment.rs — do NOT edit them. YOUR FILES: src/memory.rs (add `pub mod memory;` to src/lib.rs — the only edit there), src/bin/memory_bench.rs, results/memory.json; `cargo add` deps as needed (one at a time, re-run cargo check after each; if a crate fails to build on this Windows GNU toolchain, remove it and report).

Implement:
1. `pub trait MemoryIndex { fn add(&mut self, id: u64, v: &[f32]); fn search(&self, q: &[f32], k: usize) -> Vec<(u64, f32)>; fn len(&self) -> usize; fn bytes(&self) -> usize; }` (cosine similarity on normalised vectors).
2. Backends: `FlatIndex` (exact brute force, f32 — the ground truth), `TurbovecIndex` wrapping crates.io `turbovec` (IdMapIndex::new(dim, bit_width), add_with_ids, search — source for reference at C:\Users\mariu\crates\math-computational-100\src\turbovec-1.0.0\src\id_map.rs), and `HnswIndex` wrapping `hnsw_rs` or `instant-distance` (whichever builds). A `SharedMemory` wrapper (Arc<RwLock<Box<dyn MemoryIndex + Send + Sync>>>) so many agents/threads can read concurrently.
3. memory_bench (release mode): synthetic clustered embeddings (seeded), dim 384, N in {10k, 100k}, 1k queries, k=10. Report per backend: build time, mean & p99 query latency, recall@10 vs FlatIndex, approximate memory bytes, and concurrent throughput with 8 reader threads. Write results/memory.json and print a table.
4. Unit tests: exact search correctness for FlatIndex; recall@10 >= 0.9 for the approximate backends on a small set (or report what they achieve); concurrent read safety.
Run cargo test --lib memory and the bench. Do not git commit.

Final report (concise): backends that built, the results table, recommended default and why (honest trade-off), API summary.

handback.t:
## Shared memory: results

Everything is implemented. `cargo test --lib memory` passes 5/5 in both debug and release, and the full bench ran with release settings. Nothing was committed.

**Recommended default: `HnswIndex` (M16) at ef_search 64.** At N=100k it gives 0.976 recall in 0.52 ms, versus 4.0 ms for the exact scan, about 7.7x faster. The cost is memory: ~6.2 KB per vector, 4x the flat index. Build is also slow, 11.7 s for 100k. If RAM or build time matters more than recall, use `turbovec-4bit+rerank4x` instead (see below).

### Backends that built
On this Windows GNU toolchain:
- **`turbovec` 1.0.0** builds.
- **`hnsw_rs` 0.3.4** builds and is the one I used, because it supports adding one vector at a time.
- `instant-distance` also built, but I removed it again because it can only build an index from the whole dataset at once.
- I also added **`rayon`**, which the bench uses to measure turbovec latency on one thread.

### Results
- **Setup:** dim 384, 1k queries, k=10, seed 42.
- **Data:** a two-level clustered mixture, 64 topics × 16 subtopics; queries are new draws from the same mixture.
- **Latency:** the mean and p99 columns are single-thread, single-query. The "pool" column lets turbovec spread one query across all cores.
- **Memory:** heap bytes are measured with a counting allocator, not estimated.
- **Throughput:** 8 reader threads sharing one `SharedMemory`.
- **Full data:** `results/memory.json`.

Other agents were compiling on the same 16-thread machine during the run, so p99 and the pool column are noisy. For example, HNSW's pool numbers should equal its serial ones but don't. Treat differences under about 1.5x as noise. These are one seed on synthetic data, not real embeddings.

### Choosing a backend
- **HNSW** is the only option here that is clearly faster than flat at 100k without hurting recall. At ef64 it does 8.1k qps with 8 readers, against 450 for flat. `ef_search` can be changed while the index is in use (`ef_handle()`).
  - It uses the most memory.
  - Build is slow.
  - It cannot delete vectors.
  - At 10k it is no faster than flat; `hnsw_rs` has a lot of per-query overhead.
- **turbovec-4bit+rerank4x** is the other choice: exact recall (1.000) at 100k.
  - Its build is ~40x faster than HNSW (0.29 s vs 11.7 s).
  - It uses ~2.7x less memory than HNSW: 227 MB against 616 MB, though more than flat because it keeps a full-precision copy for re-ranking.
  - Its catch: per query it is 3x slower than HNSW, and throughput with 8 readers is about half.
- **turbovec without re-ranking** stores vectors at 7–12x less memory than flat, but recall drops as N grows (0.845 at 4-bit, 0.557 at 2-bit at 100k). It is only usable for a coarse first pass.
- **FlatIndex** is the right choice at 10k or fewer vectors, where it is exact and nearly as fast as anything else.

### API (`src/memory.rs`)
- **Trait:** `pub trait MemoryIndex { add, search, len, bytes }`, as specified. I added three provided methods: `is_empty`, `add_batch(ids, row_major)` and `name()`. Similarity is cosine; every backend normalises vectors on add and on query.
- **Backends:**
  - `FlatIndex::new(dim)` / `with_capacity`
  - `TurbovecIndex::new(dim, bits)` and `TurbovecIndex::with_rerank(dim, bits, factor)`. `dim` must be a multiple of 8 and bits must be 2–4.
  - `HnswIndex::new(dim, HnswParams{m, ef_construction, ef_search, max_elements})`, with `set_ef_search` and `ef_handle()` for live tuning.
    - It uses its own `CosineDist`, because `hnsw_rs`'s built-in dot-product distance asserts `dot <= 1` and floating-point rounding can break that.
- **Sharing:** `SharedMemory::new(Box<dyn MemoryIndex + Send + Sync>)` is a cloneable `Arc<RwLock<..>>`. It has `search`, `add`, `add_batch`, `len`, `bytes`, `name`, and `read()` to hold one lock across a batch of queries.
- **Helpers:** `recall_at_k`, `dot`, `normalized`, and `synth::{Rng, Clustered::new, Clustered::hierarchical}` (seeded, no extra dependencies).
- **Ids:** must be unique; re-adding an id is not handled as an update.

### Tests
- Exact correctness: FlatIndex against a naive full sort (using dim 40 to exercise the leftover-element path), and a stored vector finding itself as top-1.
- Recall on 3000 vectors at dim 128:
  - HNSW 0.978–0.990, asserted ≥ 0.9.
  - turbovec 4-bit+rerank 1.000, asserted ≥ 0.9.
  - Plain turbovec 4-bit 0.900 and 2-bit 0.616; for these I only assert lower floors of 0.5 and 0.3.
- Adding vectors one at a time works for every backend.
- Concurrency: 8 reader threads get the same results as a single thread for each backend; a writer inserting while 4 threads read causes no panics.

- `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\memory.json`
- `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\src\lib.rs` — only change is `pub mod memory;`.
- `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\Cargo.toml` — added turbovec, hnsw_rs and rayon.

One build note: partway through, the lib briefly failed to compile because of another agent's in-progress edit to `src/sim.rs`. It compiled again on a retry, and that is when the full bench ran.
